title: The True Vine, Friends of Jesus, and the Hatred of the World
summary: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the keeper of the vineyard, and he urges the disciples to remain in him, since a branch cut off from the vine bears no fruit and is fit only for the fire. He commands them to love one another as he has loved them, and he calls them no longer servants but friends, chosen and appointed to bear lasting fruit. He warns that the world will hate them as it hated him, and he promises that the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, will testify about him, as they also must.
story:
Chapter 14 ended with Jesus rising from the table: “Get up! Let us go on from here” (14:31). Chapter 15 continues the farewell teaching without a new scene, and 18:1 is the next place the narrator says they went out. Whether Jesus spoke these words still in the room, on the walk through the city, or (as some older readers imagined) passing the vines on the way to the Kidron, John does not say.

Where chapter 14 answered the disciples' fear of his leaving with promises (a place prepared, the Spirit's coming, his peace), chapter 15 turns to how they are to live in the time between: joined to him as branches to a vine, joined to one another in the love he has shown, and set against a world that will treat them as it treated him. The chapter moves in three steps. It begins with union and fruit (verses 1 to 8), deepens into love and friendship (9 to 17), and then turns sharply to hatred and persecution (18 to 25), before ending with the third Advocate saying: the Spirit and the disciples together will testify about Jesus (26 and 27). The movement from intimacy to opposition is deliberate. The love that binds the disciples to Jesus is the same thing that sets them apart from the world, and chapter 16 will make the threat concrete.
historical:
The vine was one of the most familiar symbols of Israel in Jesus' day, not only in Scripture but in stone and metal. Herod's temple, rebuilt from about 20 or 19 BC, carried a great golden vine above the entrance to the sanctuary. Josephus describes it twice: in the Antiquities as a golden vine with hanging clusters over the gate (Antiquities 15.395), and in the Jewish War as golden vines with clusters as tall as a man (Jewish War 5.210). The Mishnah remembers that worshipers who wished to give a freewill offering brought a golden leaf, grape, or cluster, and the priests hung it on the vine (m. Middot 3:8). The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around AD 110, reports that because a golden vine had been found in the temple some Romans concluded that the Jews worshiped Liber, the wine god, a conclusion he himself rejected (Histories 5.5). The rebels of the First Jewish Revolt minted bronze coins with a vine leaf in its second year (AD 67 to 68), and the coins of the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132 to 135) carry a grape cluster and vine leaves. When Jesus said “I am the true vine,” his hearers knew the vine as a national emblem, carved over the door of the house of God.

Jewish writing of the period uses the image in ways that bear on this chapter. In the apocalypse known as 2 Baruch, written after the destruction of the temple in AD 70, a vision of a forest, a vine, and a fountain is interpreted as the coming dominion of God's Anointed, which is like the fountain and the vine (2 Baruch 36 to 39, especially 39:7). The Didache, an early Christian manual from around AD 100 or earlier, gives thanks at the eucharistic meal for the holy vine of David made known through Jesus (Didache 9:2). And a later rabbinic saying attributed to Resh Lakish compares Israel to a vine whose branches, clusters, and leaves stand for different kinds of people in the nation (b. Hullin 92a).

The second half of the chapter looks ahead to what Jesus' followers would suffer. The book of Acts records arrests and floggings by the temple authorities (Acts 4 to 5), the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7), and the execution of James the son of Zebedee by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2). Josephus reports that James the brother of Jesus was stoned in AD 62 on the order of the high priest Ananus (Antiquities 20.200). Roman hostility followed. Tacitus says that after the fire of Rome in AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians, whom the people already hated, and put many to death, and he describes them as convicted less of arson than of hatred of the human race (Annals 15.44). Around AD 112 the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to handle the Christians of Bithynia, some of whom he had executed simply for persisting in the name (Letters 10.96). By the time John's Gospel circulated, Jesus' words about being hated for his name described what many readers already knew.
cultural:
Vineyards covered the terraced hillsides of Judea and Galilee, and every listener knew their work. Vines were pruned hard in the dormant season, when the dead and weak wood was cut away, and again in the growing season, when unwanted shoots were pinched off so the plant's strength went into grapes rather than leaves (Leviticus 25:3 and Isaiah 18:5 mention pruning; Isaiah 5:1-7 describes the whole labor of planting, clearing, and guarding). The keeper of the vineyard (geōrgos, literally a worker of the ground) is the one who does all this. Vine wood itself was useless for building or carving: Ezekiel 15:1-8 asks whether anyone makes even a peg from it, and answers that it is good only for fuel. A branch had life only while it stayed joined to the stock.

Friendship in the ancient world carried more than private affection. Hellenistic kings had an inner circle formally called their Friends, trusted advisers who knew the king's mind, and 1 Maccabees records that Jonathan the Hasmonean was enrolled among the king's chief Friends (1 Maccabees 10:65); the title friend of Caesar in John 19:12 belongs to the same world. A slave, by contrast, carried out orders without being told the reasons. Scripture calls Abraham the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8, 2 Chronicles 20:7, James 2:23) and says the LORD spoke with Moses face to face as a man speaks with his friend (Exodus 33:11). Greek moral philosophy prized friendship highly. Aristotle devotes two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to it (books 8 and 9) and says the good man will do much for his friends and, if need be, die for them (9.8), and in Plato's Symposium (179b) a speaker praises lovers as the only ones willing to die for each other. Jesus' saying that no one has greater love than to lay down one's life for one's friends would have sounded like the highest ideal of that world, but he speaks it of an act he will perform within hours.

The language of hatred and persecution also reflects social reality. In a society built on kinship, synagogue, and guild, loyalty to a crucified man cost standing, and the word Jesus uses for the world's claim on its own (idion, verse 19) is the language of family belonging. Remember the word I spoke to you (verse 20) points back to the saying at the foot washing that no servant is greater than his master (13:16), a proverb any household would recognize.
literary:
The chapter opens with the seventh and last of John's I am sayings with a predicate: “I am the true vine” (verse 1), repeated in verse 5, after the bread (6:35), the light (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), and the way, the truth, and the life (14:6). The image is not a parable with a plot but an extended metaphor that Jesus interprets as he goes, much like the shepherd discourse in chapter 10, which John calls a figure of speech (paroimia, 10:6). The adjective true (alēthinos) is one John uses for the real thing to which earlier things pointed: the true light (1:9), the true bread from heaven (6:32), and in 17:3 the only true God.

The first half is bound together by the verb remain (menō), used eleven times in verses 4 to 16, and by fruit (karpos), used eight times. Verses 2 and 3 contain a play on words that English can barely show: the Father prunes (kathairei) every fruitful branch, and the disciples are already clean (katharoi) through the word Jesus has spoken, recalling the foot washing, where Jesus told them they were clean, though not all of them (13:10-11). The second section (9 to 17) is framed by an inclusio, a repetition that opens and closes a unit: the command to love one another as he has loved them (verse 12) and “This is My command to you: Love one another” (verse 17). At its center stands the saying about laying down one's life for friends (verse 13).

The third section (18 to 25) turns on the verb hate (miseō), used seven times, and on a set of if clauses that trace the world's response back to its source: if the world hates you, it hated me first; if you were of the world, it would love its own; if they persecuted me, they will persecute you; if I had not come and spoken, they would not have sin. The section ends with a formula of fulfillment. “They hated Me without reason” (verse 25) echoes the complaint of the righteous sufferer in Psalm 35:19 and 69:4, and John calls the Psalms their Law, using the word for Israel's Scriptures as a whole, as he does at 10:34 and 12:34. Psalm 69 is one of John's favorite psalms of the suffering righteous one (compare 2:17 and 19:28-29). The chapter's last two verses form a hinge to chapter 16: the Advocate will testify, and you also must testify, so that the courtroom language of witness, which runs through the whole Gospel from the Baptist's testimony in chapter 1, now passes to the Spirit and the disciples together.

outline.t: The vine and the branches: remain in me
Remain in my love: friends of Jesus
The Spirit and the disciples will testify

doctrines.note: The vine and branches is the Gospel's fullest picture of union with Christ: “Remain in Me, and I will remain in you” (verse 4). The union is mutual, it is the source of all fruit (“apart from Me you can do nothing,” verse 5), it is kept by his words remaining in the disciples (verse 7), and it takes the shape of love and obedience rather than of mystical absorption (verses 9 and 10).

The love of the Father for the Son is the source, the Son's love for the disciples is the channel, and their love for one another is the result (verses 9 and 12). Jesus defines the measure of that love by his own death for his friends (verse 13), so that the command to love one another as he has loved them is a command to self-giving, not to sentiment.

Verses 2 and 6 warn that a branch that does not remain is thrown away, withers, and is burned, while verse 16 grounds the disciples' fruit in Jesus' choosing. Christians read the warning and the promise together in different ways, some holding that true branches will be kept to the end and others that a real branch can be lost; see the hard question below.

“If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (verse 18). Jesus prepares his followers for opposition as the ordinary result of belonging to him and being chosen out of the world (verse 19), not as a sign that something has gone wrong. The hatred is directed at his name (verse 21) and, through him, at the Father (verse 23).

The Advocate is “the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father,” whom Jesus will send from the Father, and his work is to testify about Jesus (verse 26). The verse's phrase proceeds from the Father entered the creed of 381 and later became the center of the East-West dispute over the filioque, the Western addition saying that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Both churches confess the Spirit as fully God.

words.note: Ampelos, vine. It occurs nine times in the New Testament: three times in Jesus' words at the Last Supper about the fruit of the vine (Matthew 26:29, Mark 14:25, Luke 22:18), three times here (verses 1, 4, 5), once in James 3:12, and twice in the vision of the harvest of the earth's vine in Revelation 14:18-19. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew gefen, the vine that stands for Israel in Psalm 80:8 and Hosea 10:1. The word is ordinary; its weight here comes from that long history of Israel as God's vine.

Menō, to remain, stay, abide, continue. It occurs about 118 times in the New Testament, some 40 of them in John and more than 20 in 1 John, making it one of the most characteristic words of the Johannine writings. In John it can mean simply staying in a place (1:39) but more often describes a settled relationship: the Spirit remaining on Jesus (1:32), the Father remaining in the Son (14:10), believers remaining in Jesus' word (8:31). Used eleven times in this chapter, it names continuance in a relationship already given, not an effort to achieve one.

Karpos, fruit. It occurs about 66 times in the New Testament, ten of them in John, eight in this chapter. In Scripture fruit often stands for the visible outcome of a life, good or bad (Isaiah 5:2-4, Matthew 7:16-20), and Paul speaks of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23). Here it includes the love and obedience Jesus describes in verses 9 to 17, and the language of going and bearing fruit that remains (verse 16), together with the harvest image of 4:36 and 12:24, suggests the fruit of mission as well. John does not separate the two.

Kathairō, to clean or prune. It occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 2). In agricultural Greek it was used of clearing a vine of unwanted growth, and its cognate adjective katharos, clean, appears in verse 3: the Father prunes (kathairei) the fruitful branches, and the disciples are already clean (katharoi) because of Jesus' word. The play links pruning to the cleansing Jesus spoke of at the foot washing (13:10) and makes his word, not only hardship, the instrument by which the Father makes his people fruitful.

Philos, friend. It occurs 29 times in the New Testament, six in John (3:29, 11:11, 15:13-15, 19:12), and is related to the verb phileō, to love. In the Greek world friends shared confidences and possessions, and the Friends of a king were his trusted inner circle. Jesus calls the disciples friends because he has made known to them all he heard from the Father (verse 15), yet they are friends if they do what he commands (verse 14). Friendship does not cancel his lordship; it changes obedience from a slave's compliance into the shared purpose of those who know his mind.

Eklegō, to choose, select. It occurs 22 times in the New Testament and five in John (6:70, 13:18, 15:16 twice, 15:19), always of Jesus choosing the disciples. In the Greek Old Testament it is the ordinary word for God's choosing of Israel, of Jerusalem, and of David (Deuteronomy 7:6-7 uses the idea). In verse 16 the choice is for a purpose, to go and bear fruit, and in verse 19 it is the reason the world hates them: Jesus has chosen them out of the world. The same word marks Judas in 6:70, so John does not treat being chosen as a guarantee apart from remaining.

Miseō, to hate. It occurs about 40 times in the New Testament and twelve in John, seven of them in verses 18 to 25. In Semitic idiom hate can mean to love less or to set aside (Genesis 29:31, Luke 14:26), but here it means active hostility, the dark counterpart of the Father's love. John traces the hatred to its root: those who hate Jesus hate his Father (verse 23), and they hate without cause, as the psalmist said (verse 25).

Martureō, to testify, bear witness. It is one of John's key words, occurring about 33 times in the Gospel (76 in the New Testament), far more than in any other book. The Gospel is built like a trial in which witnesses testify to Jesus: the Baptist (1:7), the Father (5:37), Jesus' works (10:25), and the Scriptures (5:39). In verses 26 and 27 the Spirit and the disciples take up the testimony after Jesus leaves, and the qualification for the disciples is that they have been with him from the beginning, the standard Acts 1:21-22 also uses for an apostle.

christ:
In the Old Testament Israel was God's vine, brought out of Egypt and planted in the land (Psalm 80:8), tended with care but yielding wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1-7), a choice vine turned degenerate (Jeremiah 2:21), a luxuriant vine that produced fruit for itself (Hosea 10:1), fit in its fruitlessness only for the fire (Ezekiel 15). Psalm 80 is especially suggestive. After lamenting the ravaged vine it prays for the man at God's right hand, the son of man God raised up for himself (80:17), so that the vine and a single representative figure already stand side by side. When Jesus says he is the true vine, he claims to be what Israel was called to be, the faithful people of God gathered up in one person who bears the fruit God looked for. The claim does not erase Israel. Jesus and the disciples he addresses are Israelites, and those who remain in him become branches of Israel's vine, a picture Paul makes with a different plant when he speaks of Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17-24). How far this fulfillment language implies replacement is debated; see the hard question below.

The chapter also shows Christ as the one whose love is the pattern and source of his people's love. He loves the disciples as the Father has loved him (verse 9), keeps his Father's commandments as they are to keep his (verse 10), and defines love by laying down his life for his friends (verse 13), spoken on the night before he did it. He is the friend who shares the Father's mind (verse 15) and the Lord who chooses and appoints (verse 16). And he is the rejected righteous one of the Psalms. By applying Psalm 69:4 to himself (verse 25), he places his coming death within Israel's prayers of the innocent sufferer, the same psalm the disciples remembered at the temple (2:17) and that John will recall at the cross (19:28-29). Finally, the Son sends the Spirit from the Father (verse 26), so that his work continues through the Spirit's witness and his people's after his departure.
interpretation:
The fathers read the vine as a picture of Christ and his church. John Chrysostom (Homilies 76 and 77 on John) took the image to teach that believers can do nothing without Christ's power and must be joined to him by faith as a branch to its stock. Augustine's Tractates on John 80 to 92 cover the chapter. In Tractate 80 he explains that Christ is the vine as mediator, the man Christ Jesus who is head of the church, and in Tractate 81 he presses verse 5 against the Pelagians: Jesus did not say that without him we can do little, but nothing. The Council of Carthage in 418 cited the verse in one of its canons against Pelagius's teaching, and the Second Council of Orange (529) devoted its twenty-fourth canon to the branches of the vine, which receive life from the vine and give nothing to it. Verse 26 had its own history. The creed of the Council of Constantinople (381) confessed the Spirit as proceeding from the Father in words drawn from this verse. Augustine (On the Trinity 15.26.47) taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father principally and also from the Son, and Western churches began adding filioque, and the Son, to the creed in Spain, where it is associated with the Council of Toledo in 589 (the manuscript evidence for its first appearance there is debated). Photius of Constantinople's Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit in the ninth century argued from this verse that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. The creed with the filioque was sung at a papal Mass in Rome in 1014, at the coronation of the emperor Henry II, and the question remained at the heart of the division between East and West.

Medieval art made the chapter visible. The twelfth-century apse mosaic of San Clemente in Rome shows the cross growing from a great vine whose scrolls fill the apse, with an inscription likening the church of Christ to this vine, and Byzantine and later Orthodox icons of Christ the True Vine seat the apostles in the branches around him. The Reformers read the chapter as a text on grace and assurance. Calvin's commentary (1553) stresses that fruitfulness comes wholly from Christ and treats the fruitless branches as those who appear to be in Christ without being rooted in him, while John Wesley's Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (1755) read verse 6 as a warning that a real branch can be cut off. The debate between the Remonstrants and the Synod of Dort (1618 to 1619) over perseverance drew on the chapter from both sides.

In the nineteenth century the chapter shaped a movement of devotional writing on abiding. The missionary Hudson Taylor, in 1869, found in a letter from his colleague John McCarthy the thought of resting in Christ rather than striving, and the vine became the center of what his biographers called the exchanged life. Andrew Murray's The True Vine, a month of meditations on 15:1-16, carried the same teaching widely. Bruce Wilkinson's Secrets of the Vine (2001) popularized the reading of airō in verse 2 as lifting up a trailing branch, a reading most commentators, including D. A. Carson, have not accepted. Modern critical scholarship has asked how the vine relates to the eucharistic words about the fruit of the vine; Raymond Brown's Anchor Bible commentary (1970) and others have suggested that John's discourse may echo eucharistic language, since John has no institution narrative, while others think the link is too slender to carry weight.

Verse 13 took on a public life of its own. Many memorials to the dead of the First World War carry it, and John Ireland's anthem Greater Love Hath No Man (1912), which sets words from the Song of Songs, this chapter, 1 Peter, 1 Corinthians, and Romans, became a staple of remembrance services. In the Revised Common Lectionary verses 1 to 8 are read on the fifth Sunday of Easter and verses 9 to 17 on the sixth Sunday of Easter in Year B, and verses 26 and 27, with 16:4b-15, on the Day of Pentecost in Year B. In the older Western lectionary 15:26 to 16:4 was the Gospel for Exaudi, the Sunday after the Ascension. In the Orthodox Church the whole chapter is part of the first of the Twelve Passion Gospels read at the service of Holy Thursday evening.
text:
Most differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from translation. In verse 1 the King James Version's ‘husbandman’ is an older word for the farmer or vinedresser (geōrgos); the BSB has ‘keeper of the vineyard’. In verse 2 the KJV has ‘taketh away’ and ‘purgeth’, and modern versions ‘cuts off’ or ‘takes away’ and ‘prunes’. The first verb (airō) normally means to lift or to remove, and a minority reading takes it here as ‘lifts up’, which is why the verse has been debated; the second (kathairō) means to cleanse or prune. In verse 15 some modern versions translate doulos as ‘slave’ rather than ‘servant’, which makes the contrast with friends sharper. In verse 26 the KJV's ‘Comforter’ and modern versions' ‘Advocate’, ‘Helper’, or ‘Counselor’ all render paraklētos.

A few manuscript differences also show in the King James Version. In verse 7 the best manuscripts have an imperative, ask whatever you wish, where later manuscripts have a future, ‘ye shall ask what ye will’. In verse 8 the earlier text reads a subjunctive, that you bear much fruit and prove to be my disciples, where later manuscripts have ‘so shall ye be my disciples’. In verse 11 the earliest manuscripts read that my joy may be in you, where later manuscripts have ‘might remain in you’, perhaps under the influence of the chapter's key verb. None of these changes the sense much.

The quotation in verse 25 matches the wording of the Greek Old Testament in two psalms, Psalm 35:19 and Psalm 69:4, both of which speak of those who hate the psalmist without cause. Psalm 69:4 is verse 5 in the Hebrew Bible, and in the Greek Old Testament, which numbers the psalms differently, the two are Psalm 34:19 and Psalm 68:5.

teach.big: Life and fruit come only from remaining in Jesus, the true vine, and the love that joins his people to him and to one another is the same love that marks them out, and exposes them, in a world that hated him first.

outline.t: Jesus is the true vine that Israel was meant to be, and the Father works on every branch, removing the fruitless and pruning the fruitful through Jesus' word.
Remaining is the whole secret of fruit: branches do not produce life, they receive it, and apart from Jesus there is nothing that lasts.
When his words remain in us, prayer becomes asking for what he wants, and the Father is glorified as disciples bear fruit.
Jesus' love for us mirrors the Father's love for him, obedience is how we stay in that love, and its goal is joy made complete.
The command to love is measured by the cross, and Jesus makes his servants friends by sharing with them what the Father has shown him.
Fruitfulness rests on his choice, not ours: he chose and appointed us to go, to bear lasting fruit, and to love one another.
Opposition is the normal lot of those chosen out of the world, because it hated him first and does not know the Father.
Jesus' words and works leave no excuse, and the hatred he met fulfills the prayers of Israel's innocent sufferer.
The Spirit and the church bear witness together, and the church's witness rests on having been with Jesus.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns remain into a technique or a feeling to be worked up, so that believers anxiously ask whether they are abiding enough. In the chapter remaining is defined by Jesus' words remaining in us, by obedience, and by love (verses 7, 10, and 12), and the initiative is his: he chose them and made them clean. The second turns verse 7 into a blank check for any request. The promise is given to those in whom his words remain, and 16:23-24 and 1 John 5:14 tie it to asking in his name and according to his will. The third treats fruit as a number, whether converts or programs, and then measures people by it. Fruit includes love and obedience, and some of the most fruitful branches are the least visible.

The fourth pitfall is to identify pruning with every hardship and to tell a suffering person that God is cutting them back. Verse 3 names the word Jesus has spoken as the means of cleansing, and while hardship can be one of God's instruments (Hebrews 12:5-11), the text does not license that interpretation of someone else's grief. The fifth uses verse 6 either to threaten believers with damnation for every lapse or to explain it away entirely; teachers should let the warning stand and state honestly that traditions read it differently. The sixth reads the world of verses 18 to 25, or their Law in verse 25, as the Jewish people. In John the world is humanity organized against God, including Romans and in time some who call themselves Christians; Jesus and the eleven are Jews, and the psalm he quotes is Israel's own prayer. Finally, the persecution passage is misused when Christians treat every criticism as persecution for righteousness' sake. Jesus speaks of hatred because of my name (verse 21), not of the consequences of Christians' own failures.
teach.pastoral: The pruning image will press on people who are suffering, and it must be handled with restraint. Some have been told that God took a child or a marriage in order to make them more fruitful, and have found the words crushing. It is better to say what the text says: the Father's work on the branches is purposeful and aimed at life, and Jesus' word already makes his disciples clean. The warning in verse 6 will trouble the scrupulous, who fear that their weakness proves they were never truly branches. Remind them that the chapter's command is to remain, that is, to keep coming back to the one who chose them, and that Jesus spoke these words to men who would all desert him that night and whom he restored. For people who have been rejected by family or community because of their faith, verses 18 to 21 offer company: they are not odd or cursed, and Jesus went there first. Those who have been hurt by Christians should hear that the world's hatred Jesus describes has sometimes worn the church's clothes, and that the command in this chapter is love.

hard.q: Branches that do not remain are thrown into the fire. Can a true believer be cut off and lost?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the objection to any doctrine of eternal security comes from the chapter itself. Verse 2 speaks of a branch in Me that bears no fruit and is cut off, and verse 6 of anyone who does not remain being thrown away and burned. The natural reading, its defenders say, is that these were real branches, genuinely joined to Christ, who ceased to remain. John Wesley's Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (1755) took it so, and I. Howard Marshall's Kept by the Power of God (1969) argued at length that the New Testament's warnings, including this one, describe a real possibility of apostasy for those who have truly believed. The Council of Trent (1547) taught that no one can know with absolute certainty, apart from special revelation, that they will persevere to the end, while affirming perseverance as a great gift of God. Wesleyan, Arminian, Catholic, and Orthodox readers generally agree that a believer can, by persistent unbelief, cease to remain in Christ.

Augustine (On the Gift of Perseverance, about 429) and the Reformed tradition answer differently. They read the passage alongside Jesus' promise that no one will snatch his sheep from his hand (10:28-29) and his words in this chapter that he chose the disciples and appointed their fruit (verse 16). The Canons of Dort (1619) and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 17) hold that those truly united to Christ will be kept by God to the end, and they read the fruitless branches as those with an outward connection to Jesus but no living union, as Judas had, whom Jesus also chose (6:70) and who had just gone out into the night (13:30). Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday (The Race Set Before Us, 2001) argue that the warnings are the very means by which God keeps his people, so that the warning is real and the keeping is sure. A third reading, associated with Zane Hodges and others in the Free Grace tradition, takes the burning as a picture of a believer's life becoming useless and suffering loss, not of eternal judgment. A fourth approach reads airō in verse 2 as lifting up rather than cutting off, though most commentators, including D. A. Carson, think cutting off suits the context and verse 6 better.

Every reading agrees on the chapter's aim: life comes only from remaining in Christ, and the warning is meant to drive disciples to him, not to make them look away from him to examine themselves endlessly. Whether a true believer can finally fall away is a second-order question on which faithful churches have disagreed since the fifth century.

hard.q: When Jesus calls himself the true vine, does he mean that the church has replaced Israel?
hard.a:
The objection is pressed most sharply by Jewish readers and by Christian scholars who have studied the history of Christian contempt for Judaism. The vine was Israel's emblem, carved over the temple door; to call Jesus the true vine, and then to speak of the world's hatred in their Law (verse 25), can sound like a declaration that Israel was the false vine and that the church now owns its Scriptures. Rosemary Radford Ruether (Faith and Fratricide, 1974) argued that anti-Judaism was built into the church's christology from the start, and that fulfillment language of this kind is its core. Adele Reinhartz, in The Jewish Annotated New Testament and Cast Out of the Covenant (2018), has shown how John's language was heard for centuries as a verdict on Jews as such, and that history, from medieval preaching to the violence of the Crusades and after, gives the objection its weight.

Several responses have been made, and they do not all agree. Many commentators, among them C. K. Barrett and Raymond Brown, note that true in John means the reality to which earlier things pointed, as with the true bread in 6:32, which does not make the manna false; and that Psalm 80 already joins the vine to a single man at God's right hand (80:17), so that Jesus embodies Israel rather than replacing it. On this view the branches are joined to Israel's vine, not transplanted into a different one, a reading close to Paul's image of Gentiles grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17-24). Others, including N. T. Wright, read the passage as Israel's vocation fulfilled in its Messiah and opened to the nations, while R. Kendall Soulen (The God of Israel and Christian Theology, 1996) has urged Christians to abandon supersessionism, the teaching that the church has simply replaced Israel, in favor of an account in which God's covenant with the Jewish people continues. The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the idea that Jews are rejected or accursed by God.

The text itself sets some limits. The speaker and all his hearers are Jews, the quotation in verse 25 is Israel's own lament, and the world in John is humanity in revolt against God, not a nation. How exactly the fulfillment Jesus claims relates to God's continuing purpose for Israel is a question Christians still answer in more than one way; what is not in question is that the chapter gives no warrant for hatred, since its command is to love.

observe: What does the keeper of the vineyard do with fruitless branches and with fruitful ones (verse 2), and what reason does verse 3 give for the disciples being clean?
How many times does the word remain appear in verses 4 to 10, and what different things are said to remain?
What three reasons does Jesus give in verses 18 to 21 for the world's hatred?
interpret: Why does Jesus call himself the true vine? How does the Old Testament use of the vine for Israel shape what he is claiming?
What changes when Jesus calls his disciples friends rather than servants, and what stays the same (verses 14 and 15)?
How do the warning of verse 6 and the promise of verse 16 fit together?
apply: Where are you trying to bear fruit in your own strength, and what would it look like to remain in Jesus there?
Jesus defines love by laying down his life for his friends. Who is one person for whom love would cost you something this week?
Have you experienced opposition because of Jesus' name? How can you tell the difference between that and the consequences of your own faults?
